beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Chaitanya, and this video is about how the Memory API lets the tutor remember a student across different textbooks.

show.event: Paper fill, deck rail present
MEMORY API slams in, Archivo Black
Sign-in lede rises beneath, accent on the key phrase

beats.note: The only beat with no counterpart in the deck. Built in the deck's own CSS so it is indistinguishable in style; no new framing introduced.

beats.narration_text: A student spends a whole semester in one textbook. The tutor learns how they think — where they're solid, where they get stuck. Next semester they open a different book. And the tutor there has never heard of them. That's what the Memory API exists to fix. Two endpoints, two tables. It's small, and it's the difference between a tutor and a search box with a chat bubble.

show.event: Kicker rises: MEDHAVY HUB / MEMORY API
THE TUTOR FORGETS slams in
Lede rises, 'stranger' highlighted in accent

beats.narration_text: There are two tables, doing genuinely different jobs. chat_memory_turns is short-term. One row per message, tagged user or assistant. It's the transcript — what lets the tutor understand 'what about the other one?' as a follow-up instead of a brand new question. learner_profiles is long-term. One row per student, holding untyped JSON. Topics they've seen, gaps they've shown, how deep they like explanations. A transcript is what was said. A profile is what the tutor concluded.

show.event: TWO TABLES wipes in
chat_memory_turns box rises, white
learner_profiles box rises, filled black
Note rises: different lifetimes, different jobs

beats.narration_text: Both tables key on the same field — memory_subject. This is the most important idea here, and it's easy to miss, because it's just a string. The hub treats it as opaque. With one exception: if the subject starts with hub:, the profile route slices that off and stores the Clerk user ID separately. That convention is the entire cross-book mechanism. Two books using the same subject share one memory. Two books using different subjects are strangers. There's no identity resolution happening. It's a naming convention — and it works exactly as far as every book follows it.

show.event: ONE STRING HOLDS IT UP wipes in
keyline slams: hub: in accent, user_abc123 beside it
BOTH TABLES callout rises
hub: PREFIX callout rises
THE WHOLE TRICK callout rises

beats.narration_text: Every exchange gets posted as a pair — the question and the answer. Then it prunes. It keeps the most recent twenty-four turns, forty-eight rows, and deletes everything older for that subject. So short-term memory is genuinely short. It's a rolling window, not an archive. If you're expecting to pull a student's full history out of this later — it isn't there.

show.event: IT FORGETS ON PURPOSE wipes in
Message tape rises, U/A pairs
The oldest four tip over and fall away
KEEP 24 TURNS -> 48 ROWS. DELETE THE REST.
Note rises: rolling window, not an archive

beats.narration_text: Now the honest part. The hub provides all of this — I read the code, it works. Whether the books actually use it is a separate question. At least one textbook's architecture doc describes storing memory in local SQLite, scoped to that book alone. If that's still current, memory isn't crossing books yet, even though the machinery for it is sitting right here. So treat this as infrastructure that's built and waiting — not a feature you can assume is live. If you're working on a book, finding out which side it's on is the first thing to check.

show.event: BUILT != WIRED wipes in
Two-panel status grid slams in
Verify-before-shipping stamp lands on the right panel, alert red, rotated
Note rises: built and waiting, not necessarily live

beats.narration_variant: PRIMARY — the alternate 'ONE STUDENT, MANY BOOKS' version was deliberately NOT used. The script flags the underlying claim as unconfirmed and the operator has not verified it.

beats.narration_text: So: two tables — a transcript and a profile. Forty-eight messages kept in a rolling window. And one string, hub: plus a user ID, that decides whether two books are talking about the same student. If you're wiring up a new book, that subject string is the thing to get right. Everything else follows from it.

show.event: THE SHAPE OF IT wipes in
02 / 48 / 01 end grid slams in
Closing lede rises, subject string highlighted
